parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: force as rate of change of momentum
hints: Hint 1: Think beyond a push or pull and focus on what happens to the momentum of an object when a resultant force acts on it over time.
parts.proper_answer: Force is the rate of change of momentum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the Fundamental Definition**
You meet $F = ma$ a lot, but that is a special case for constant mass. The more general idea that works always is that a resultant force changes momentum. So think of force as how quickly momentum is changing with time.

Step 2: **State It Precisely**
In symbols this is $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ where $p$ is momentum. So the one-line definition is: force is the rate of change of momentum.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 3.2 to read the value of $X$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.0\text{ s}$, then combine it with the $0.80\text{ N}$ resistive force to find the net forward force.
Hint 2: Remember how impulse links to momentum change, and use the $3.0\text{ s}$ time interval to turn that net force into a change in momentum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Resultant Force**
From Fig. 3.2, $X = 1.4\text{ N}$ forward from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.0\text{ s}$. The resistive force is $0.80\text{ N}$ backward at all speeds. So the resultant forward force is $$F_{net} = X - F_{res} = 1.4 - 0.80 = 0.60\text{ N}$$ A common slip is to use $1.4\text{ N}$ alone. Only the unbalanced part changes momentum.

Step 2: **Use Impulse Equals Change in Momentum**
Impulse is resultant force multiplied by time, and it equals the change in momentum: $$\Delta p = F_{net} \times \Delta t$$ Put in the numbers: $$\Delta p = 0.60 \times 3.0 = 1.8\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$ That is the gain in forward momentum over the first $3.0\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the value of $X$ from Fig. 3.2 between $3.0\text{ s}$ and $6.0\text{ s}$ with the constant $0.80\text{ N}$ resistive force.
Hint 2: Think about what Newton's first law says about motion when all the forces balance to zero.
parts.proper_answer: From $t = 3.0\text{ s}$ to $6.0\text{ s}$, $X = 0.80\text{ N}$ so resultant force is zero. Hence the block moves with constant velocity (Newton's first law).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Check the Force Balance**
From Fig. 3.2, after $t = 3.0\text{ s}$, $X = 0.80\text{ N}$ forward. The resistive force is $0.80\text{ N}$ backward. So: $$F_{net} = 0.80 - 0.80 = 0$$ The forces are exactly balanced.

Step 2: **Link Zero Resultant to Motion**
With no resultant force there is no acceleration, so momentum and velocity do not change. The block is already moving after the first $3.0\text{ s}$, so it keeps moving forward at a steady, constant velocity. This is Newton's first law in action.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on which force is doing the stated $2.0\text{ W}$ of power and read its value from Fig. 3.2 for the $3.0\text{ s}$ to $6.0\text{ s}$ interval.
Hint 2: Recall the relation linking mechanical power to force and steady velocity, and use it to find the speed of the block.
Hint 3: Convert that steady speed into a distance using the $3.0\text{ s}$ duration of this interval.
parts.proper_answer: Between $3.0\text{ s}$ and $6.0\text{ s}$, $X = 0.80\text{ N}$. $v = P/X = 2.0/0.80 = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Distance $= v \times t = 2.5 \times 3.0 = 7.5\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Power to Find Velocity**
Power from a force at steady speed is $$P = Fv$$ Here the power $P = 2.0\text{ W}$ is produced by force $X$, and $X = 0.80\text{ N}$ in this interval. Rearrange before substituting: $$v = \frac{P}{F} = \frac{2.0}{0.80} = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This works nicely because velocity is constant here.

Step 2: **Convert Velocity to Distance**
The time interval is $$\Delta t = 6.0 - 3.0 = 3.0\text{ s}$$ At constant velocity: $$s = v \times \Delta t = 2.5 \times 3.0 = 7.5\text{ m}$$

Step 3: **Alternative Check via Work**
You can think of it as total work first: $W = P \times t = 2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0\text{ J}$. Then $W = Fs$ gives $s = W/F = 6.0/0.80 = 7.5\text{ m}$. Both routes agree.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Start from rest at $t = 0$ and think about the shape of a momentum-time graph when a constant resultant force acts from $0$ to $3.0\text{ s}$.
Hint 2: Think about what must happen to momentum when the resultant force becomes zero after $3.0\text{ s}$ while the block is still moving.
parts.proper_answer: 0 to $3.0\text{ s}$: straight line of constant positive gradient starting at the origin. 3.0 to $6.0\text{ s}$: horizontal straight line at the value reached at $3.0\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sketch 0 to 3.0 s - Steady Gain**
The block starts at rest, so momentum starts at zero. From $0$ to $3.0\text{ s}$ the resultant force is constant at $0.60\text{ N}$. Since $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, a constant $F$ means momentum grows at a constant rate. So draw an upward sloping straight line from the origin to $t = 3.0\text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Sketch 3.0 to 6.0 s - No Further Change**
After $3.0\text{ s}$ the resultant force is zero, so $\Delta p = 0$. Momentum stays at the value it had at $3.0\text{ s}$. So draw a flat horizontal line from $t = 3.0\text{ s}$ to $t = 6.0\text{ s}$, with no step or drop at $3.0\text{ s}$.
